summary: Lunar Site Navigator is a web app that answers one question for any Moon landing site and date: will the lander have sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth for radio contact, and for how long? Pick up to three places, a landing date and a length of stay. The app shows the sky from the landing spot with the Sun, Earth and the real skyline, and gives each place a plain verdict (Good spot, Risky, Needs a relay satellite, or Too dark) with the numbers behind it: time in sunlight, time with Earth in view, the longest darkness, and the battery needed to get through it. For south-pole sites the skyline comes from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data, because there the Sun skims a few degrees above the horizon and a single ridge decides whether a lander gets light. Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.004°. This matters: in March 2025 the Athena lander tipped over into a shadowed crater near the south pole and its battery ran out after about 12 hours. The tool turns hard-to-use ephemeris and terrain data into a decision anyone can read in seconds.
details:
What it does

Lunar Site Navigator answers one question: if a lander touches down at this place on this date, will it have sunlight (power and warmth) and a clear line to Earth (to send its data home), and for how long? You pick up to three places (south-pole sites with real NASA terrain, past landings to compare, or your own coordinates), a landing date in UTC and a length of stay from one day to one month. Each place gets a plain verdict that names the problem: Good spot, Risky, Needs a relay satellite, or Too dark, with one sentence explaining why.

The app is laid out like a desktop tool, with tabs on the left, and fits on a laptop screen without scrolling:

  • Simulation: the sky from the landing spot, with the Sun, Earth and the real skyline. Press play to watch the stay unfold, or step through it six hours at a time. Day-by-day bands show sunlight and Earth contact for every place side by side; click them to jump in time. The verdict and key numbers for the selected place sit on the right.
  • Compare places: one table with the places side by side: verdict, reason, time in sunlight, time with Earth in view, both together, longest darkness, battery needed, solar energy per day and which horizon data was used. A banner names the best of your places.
  • Best months: a 12-month trend of sunlight and Earth contact for each place, to find the best landing window.
  • Ask AI: a local AI assistant that answers questions by running the app's own calculator (details below).
  • How it works: the question, why it matters, the method, data sources, the AI disclosure and a full glossary. Every hard term in the app also has an information button with a plain-language explanation.

How it works

  1. Where are the Sun and Earth? For every moment of the stay, the app works out where both appear in the sky from the landing spot (azimuth and elevation), using astronomy-engine with the IAU lunar rotation model and correcting for the observer's position on the Moon. It counts how much of the Sun's disc is above the skyline, not just its centre. A test suite compares the results with NASA JPL Horizons at 23 reference points (south pole, Apollo 11, Shackleton; Sun and Earth; December 2026 to June 2027). The worst difference is 0.0023° in elevation and 0.0037° in azimuth; the Sun's disc is about 0.53° wide.
  2. Are hills in the way? For south-pole sites, the app traces the real skyline in 720 directions out to 200 km from the NASA LRO LOLA polar elevation map LDEM_75S_120M (120 m per pixel), with the Moon's curvature, for a panel or antenna 2 m above the ground. Before writing anything, the build script checks the map's orientation by finding Shackleton crater's 3 to 4 km deep bowl, and it refuses to write the skylines if that check fails. Sites outside the map use a smooth Moon, and the app always says which horizon a result used.
  3. Can a lander live there? The app adds up the share of the stay with sunlight, with Earth in view and with both at once, the longest stretch of darkness, the battery needed to get through it at a chosen power use, and the solar energy one square metre of panel would make per day. Verdict rules: Good spot when sunlight and Earth are each in view at least 70% of the stay; Risky when either is between 20% and 70%; Needs a relay satellite when Earth is in view less than 20% of the time; Too dark when sunlight is under 20%.
  4. Check with NASA: a button sends the selected place and date to NASA JPL Horizons live and shows how far the app's Sun and Earth positions are from NASA's.

The AI assistant

Ask AI uses a small open-weight model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507) that runs on the user's own computer through llama.cpp or Ollama. It needs no API keys and no data leaves the machine. The model does not make up numbers: it calls the app's own calculator tools (list sites, analyse a site, compare sites, season overview), and every answer shows which calculation it ran. An answer that ran no calculation is labelled "numbers not checked". If no model is running, the panel says so and everything else still works.

Why it matters

Missions are heading to the Moon's south pole to look for water ice. There the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so hills cast long shadows and Earth often sits below the skyline. In March 2025 the Athena lander tipped over into a shadowed crater near the pole and its battery ran out after about 12 hours. Place and date can decide whether a mission gets days of science or none. Existing tools for Sun and Earth positions are powerful but hard to use; this app lets planners, students and the public screen sites and dates in seconds and see the trade-off between power and communication at a glance.

What makes it different

  • A sky view with the real skyline instead of tables of angles, so you can see why a place is dark or out of contact.
  • Verdicts that name the problem in plain words, with the numbers behind them one click away.
  • Accuracy that is tested, not assumed: an automated comparison with NASA JPL Horizons and a live check button.
  • Honest about its limits: approximate coordinates are marked, smooth-Moon results are labelled, and the AI shows its working.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy of positions and of the terrain projection, checked before any result is shown.
  • Clarity for non-experts: one question, plain verdicts, information buttons and a glossary.
  • Accessibility: every status has an icon and a word as well as a colour; keyboard and screen-reader friendly.
  • Privacy and cost: the AI runs locally with no accounts or keys.
  • Limits: terrain covers the south pole only (south of 75°S); panels are assumed upright and turning to face the Sun at 30% efficiency; heating, relay satellites and antenna masks are not modelled.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, Next.js and React; astronomy-engine for planetary and lunar positions; NASA JPL Horizons for validation and the live check; NASA LRO LOLA elevation data for the skylines; Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 served by llama.cpp or Ollama for the assistant; Phosphor icons; Poppins and Lato fonts.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

The app's code was written with SI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), and every source file carries an "AI-assisted code" header. This project description was also drafted with SI assistance. The in-app assistant is a local open-weight language model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507). No SI-generated images are used in the app. Any SI-generated image or video in the demo carries a visible watermark. No NASA logos or mission insignia are used.
